OVERVIEW

[1] The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX (the associate Appellants), citizens of India, allegedly fear members of a socio-spiritual organization known as the Dera Sacha Sauda (DSS). The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected their claims in a decision dated January 28, 2020, after finding that they have a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Mumbai.

[2] The Appellants appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), and request that the RPD's decision be set aside and substituted with a determination that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants request that the matter be referred back to a different panel of the RPD for redetermination.1
DETERMINATION

[3] The appeal is dismissed. I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.2
SUMMARY OF THE FACTS

[4] The Appellants are a family of four from Sri Ganganagar, a city located in the Indian state of Rajasthan, and include the 42-year-old principal Appellant, his 41-year-old wife, their 17-year-old son, and their 10-year-old daughter.

[5] The Appellants trace their problems with the DSS to the principal Appellant's brother-in-law who was allegedly threatened in 2007 because of statements he made against the group. A rock was thrown through the brother-in-law's window with a note warning him to stop expressing his views against the DSS and defaming their leader. The brother-in-law then began receiving telephone calls threatening that his house will be burned down if he does not apologize to the DSS.

[6] On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the principal Appellant attended his brother-in-law's XXXX XXXX and founded it looted. He claims that he was taking care of the business at the time while his brother-in-law was vacationing with his family in Canada. Neighbours informed him that they witnessed a group of 10 - 15 DSS followers outside of the XXXX shouting his brother-in-law's name and threatened to kill him if they see him again. According to the Appellants, this incident was part of wider protests by DSS followers at that time who were opposed to the trial of their leader on sexual assault charges. The brother-in-law and his family filed claims for refugee protection after this incident.

[7] The Appellants allege that they experienced three incidents with DSS followers in XXXX 2019, while they were visiting the home of the principal Appellant's mother-in-law. Specifically, unknown people attended her home during their visit on XXXX XXXX, 2019, looking for the principal Appellant's brother-in-law. Two unknown men wearing masks and wielding swords attended her house on XXXX XXXX and XXXX, 2019, while they were again visiting and threatened them.

[23] The Appellants were never the targets of the DSS in any of the alleged incidents but rather bystanders while the DSS followers were searching for the principal Appellant's brother-in-law. The principal Appellant observed that his brother-in-law's XXXX XXXX had been looted on XXXX XXXX, 2017, but the Appellants were never implicated or even directly witnessed the incident. All three of the alleged incidents in XXXX 2019 occurred at the mother-in-law's home and involved DSS followers searching for the brother-in-law. The Appellants' state the following in the BOC about the incident on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018: "unknown people attacked in search of by brother-in-law." They similarly state in the BOC that the incidents on XXXX XXXX, & XXXX, 2019, occurred "because of my brother-in-law's [...] (presently in Canada) issues with Dera Sacha Sauda."

[24] I agree with the RPD that the principal Appellant is not credible in his testimony that he was followed and received threatening calls after his brother-in-law's business was looted in XXXX 2017. He testified that: "[f]rom XXXX XXXX this continued happening, for about a year and a half, sometimes people would follow me, sometimes somebody would be coming behind me. Couple of times I was threatened over the phone (sic)." The RPD noted that there is no mention of these allegations in the BOC, and it correctly rejected the principal Appellant's attempt at attributing the omission to his previous representative. The Appellants did not file a complaint against their previous representative and did not amend the BOC to include these allegations despite being represented by new counsel at the hearing. Instead, the principal Appellant's confirmed under oath that the BOC "is complete, true and accurate."

[25] The Federal Court has held that it is reasonable to draw an adverse credibility finding based on an omission from the BOC of important aspects of a claim.13 The omission of incidents which display the agent of harms' direct interest in the Appellants after the looting of the XXXX XXXX is an important allegation to their claims, particularly since these alleged incidents bridge the large gap between the incident at the XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2017, and the incidents at the mother-in-law's home in XXXX 2019. The RPD therefore correctly rejected the principal Appellant's testimony that he was being followed and was receiving threatening telephone calls beginning in XXXX 2017.

[26] The RPD also correctly drew an adverse credibility finding from the contradictory evidence on whether the agents of harm threatened the principal Appellant after XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. The principal Appellant states the following in the BOC: "[a]fter the incident of XXXX XXXX & XXXX, 2019, I was threatened on the phone (sic) that the same will be repeated which they did with [my brother-in-law] and his family." Contrary to this statement in the BOC, when the principal Appellant was asked by the RPD member whether he received "any threats after the visit on the XXXX and XXXX?" he testified that "[n]o, I did not get a threat, but my parents got information that some people are - keep coming around the house. They keep going around, but nobody has said anything." The Appellant provided a third account as an explanation for the inconsistency that involved him receiving threats indirectly through his brother-in-law's social media accounts: "[n]o, these threats were not given on the phone. I did not get those threats directly, but through social media, [my brother-in-law] got that messages (sic)." When the RPD member pointed out that the statement in the BOC refers to the threats by telephone and not through social media, principal Appellant then insisted that "I got the threats only on XXXX and XXXX, but after XXXX I never got any threats," and attributed the inconsistency to his previous counsel.

[27] The Appellants' reliance on the Federal Court decision in Alekozai does not help resolve the inconsistencies between the principal Appellant's testimony and the BOC. The Appellants cite Alekozai for the principle that "discrepancies in testimony relied on to support a finding that the applicant lacked credibility were trivial and did not form a sufficient foundation upon which the applicant's overall credibility could be impugned."14 The discrepancy in Alekozai, however, involved a difference of one day when an event occurred between the claimant's testimony and the notes taken at the port of entry, which the Federal Court classified as trivial.15 In the present case, the principal Appellant provided contradictory evidence on the question of whether he ever followed or received threatening telephone calls, which is not a trivial discrepancy but rather a material contradiction which is central to the question of whether he was ever directly targeted by the agents of harm. Notably, he provided three various and mutually exclusive accounts in his oral testimony which are contrary to the narrative contained in the BOC. In the circumstances, given the extent of the contradictions in the four accounts presented by the principal Appellant, I am not satisfied that he was ever followed or received threatening calls after his brother-in-law's business was looted in XXXX 2017.16

[28] The objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP), notes that the headquarters of the DSS is in Sirsa, Haryana, and its followers are predominantly "lower caste Muslims and Sikhs in the states of Punja, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan."17 The most "significant support" for the DSS is in several districts of the Malwa region of Rajasthan state, where 70 percent of its adherents are found, and its strongest political support appears to be in Punjab state.18

[29] When considering the fact that the agents of harm never directly targeted the Appellants or displayed an interest in them alongside the information in the NDP that displays that the vast majority of DSS adherents are found in Punja, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan states, the evidence does not establish that the agents of harm are motivated to search for the Appellants and pursue them in Mumbai.

[30] For all of the reasons outlined above, based upon my own independent review of the evidence, I am satisfied that the first part of the Rasaratnam test has been met. The Appellants have not shown that they face either a serious possibility of persecution in Mumbai from the DSS, or, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture, a risk to their lives, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
It is reasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Mumbai

[31] I am satisfied that it is reasonable for the Appellants to seek refuge in Mumbai based on their specific circumstances and the objective evidence in the NDP. The Federal Court of Appeal has established, "a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area."19

argument_evidence.context_text: [32] The RPD considered relevant factors which inform the analysis of whether Mumbai is a reasonable IFA in the Appellants' specific circumstances, including their ability to travel to Mumbai, their language skills, their education and work experience, and the existence of a Sikh community with places of worship.

Beyond the foregoing, the objective evidence in the NDP establishes that Sikhs in India are economically and socially integrated, have the freedom to practice their religion, and can rely on local gurdwaras to access housing and other services.

Given the Appellants' education and work history, I do not accept the submission that "there is little support in the record indicating that the claimants would be able to find jobs in the cities identified for the IFAs (sic).

[22] The Appellants do not face more than a mere possibility of persecution or a risk of harm, on a balance of probabilities, because the evidence does not establish that the agents of harm have the motivation to search for them throughout India and pursue them in Mumbai.

They similarly state in the BOC that the incidents on XXXX XXXX, & XXXX, 2019, occurred "because of my brother-in-law's [...] (presently in Canada) issues with Dera Sacha Sauda."

He testified that: "[f]rom XXXX XXXX this continued happening, for about a year and a half, sometimes people would follow me, sometimes somebody would be coming behind me. Couple of times I was threatened over the phone (sic)." The RPD noted that there is no mention of these allegations in the BOC, and it correctly rejected the principal Appellant's attempt at attributing the omission to his previous representative. The Appellants did not file a complaint against their previous representative and did not amend the BOC to include these allegations despite being represented by new counsel at the hearing. Instead, the principal Appellant's confirmed under oath that the BOC "is complete, true and accurate."

[25] The Federal Court has held that it is reasonable to draw an adverse credibility finding based on an omission from the BOC of important aspects of a claim.13 The omission of incidents which display the agent of harms' direct interest in the Appellants after the looting of the XXXX XXXX is an important allegation to their claims, particularly since these alleged incidents bridge the large gap between the incident at the XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2017, and the incidents at the mother-in-law's home in XXXX 2019. REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX (the associate Appellants), citizens of India, allegedly fear members of a socio-spiritual organization known as the Dera Sacha Sauda (DSS). The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected their claims in a decision dated January 28, 2020, after finding that they have a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Mumbai.

[2] The Appellants appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), and request that the RPD's decision be set aside and substituted with a determination that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants request that the matter be referred back to a different panel of the RPD for redetermination.1
DETERMINATION

[3] The appeal is dismissed. I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.2
SUMMARY OF THE FACTS

[4] The Appellants are a family of four from Sri Ganganagar, a city located in the Indian state of Rajasthan, and include the 42-year-old principal Appellant, his 41-year-old wife, their 17-year-old son, and their 10-year-old daughter.

[5] The Appellants trace their problems with the DSS to the principal Appellant's brother-in-law who was allegedly threatened in 2007 because of statements he made against the group. A rock was thrown through the brother-in-law's window with a note warning him to stop expressing his views against the DSS and defaming their leader. The brother-in-law then began receiving telephone calls threatening that his house will be burned down if he does not apologize to the DSS.

[6] On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the principal Appellant attended his brother-in-law's XXXX XXXX and founded it looted. He claims that he was taking care of the business at the time while his brother-in-law was vacationing with his family in Canada. Neighbours informed him that they witnessed a group of 10 - 15 DSS followers outside of the XXXX shouting his brother-in-law's name and threatened to kill him if they see him again. According to the Appellants, this incident was part of wider protests by DSS followers at that time who were opposed to the trial of their leader on sexual assault charges. The brother-in-law and his family filed claims for refugee protection after this incident.

[7] The Appellants allege that they experienced three incidents with DSS followers in XXXX 2019, while they were visiting the home of the principal Appellant's mother-in-law. Specifically, unknown people attended her home during their visit on XXXX XXXX, 2019, looking for the principal Appellant's brother-in-law. Two unknown men wearing masks and wielding swords attended her house on XXXX XXXX and XXXX, 2019, while they were again visiting and threatened them.

[8] The Appellants left India for Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and filed their claims for refugee protection on XXXX XXXX, 2019.
THE RPD DECISION

[9] The RPD determined that the Appellants are neither Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection because they have a viable IFA Mumbai. The RPD made two adverse credibility findings as part of its IFA analysis. Firstly, it found that the principal Appellant was not credible in his testimony that he was "followed and threatened" by members of the DSS from XXXX 2017 to XXXX 2019, because these allegations are not contained in the Basis of Claim form (BOC). The RPD also drew an adverse inference from the inconsistent evidence on whether the principal Appellant was threatened by the agents of harm after XXXX XXXX, 2019.
NEW EVIDENCE
[10] The Appellants submit an affidavit sworn by the principal Appellant and ten news articles as new evidence in their appeal.

[11] New evidence is only admissible before the RAD if it arose after the rejection of the claims, if it was not reasonably available, or if the Appellants could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented it at the time of the rejection of their claims.3 In addition to these legislative requirements, under the Federal Court of Appeal decisions in Singh and Raza, admissibility is limited to evidence that is relevant, new, and credible.4

[12] I will consider the arguments that that the principal Appellant raises in his affidavit in addition to the submissions in the memorandum. However, to the extent that he seeks to provide new sworn evidence in his affidavit to elaborate upon or supplements his testimony before the RPD, such evidence does not meet the legislative requirements for admissibility and is therefore inadmissible. I have not identified anything in the affidavit which can be said to be evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim, that was not reasonably available, or which he could not have reasonably been expected to have presented at the time of the rejection of the claims.

[13] Five of the news articles predate the denial of the claims. The articles are dated August 26, 2017, November 24, 2017, February 11, 2018, December 5, 2018, and November 17, 2019. The Appellants have not argued that these articles were not reasonably available or that they could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented them at the time of the rejection of their claims. All five articles concern the DSS, are from daily newspapers such as The Tribune and the Hindustan Times, and are publicly available. These five articles are inadmissible since they do not meet one of the three legislative criteria for admissibility.

[15] While these five articles post-date the denial of the claims, the Appellants have not provided submissions explaining how they believe the articles are relevant. Some of these articles do not appear to even remotely relate to the Appellants' claims, such as the article concerning the treatment of people of African origin in India. The sole article which mentions DSS adherents merely mentions that the victims of a motor vehicle accident involving negligent driving were DSS followers. The two articles about covid-19 restrictions concern Punjab state, and are unrelated to Rajasthan, where the Appellants lived, or Mumbai in Maharashtra state. The Appellants have not explained the relevance of the death of Indian parliamentarian Gurdas Singh Badal to their claims. Ultimately, I have not identified anything in any of these five articles which is relevant to the Appellants' claims in my independent assessment. Accordingly, while these articles post-date the denial of the claims they are inadmissible because they are not relevant.

[16] The Appellants' request for a hearing before the RAD is denied because the new evidence is inadmissible. Hearings before the RAD are limited to circumstances when the new evidence on appeal is admissible and raises a serious issue with respect to the Appellants' credibility that is central to the decision, and if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claims.5
ISSUES
[17] The determinative issue in this appeal is the viability of an IFA in Mumbai.
STANDARD OF REVIEW

[18] The standard of correctness applies to this appeal as set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica.6 This requires an independent assessment of the refugee claims to determine whether the RPD was correct in its findings and determinations.7 While deference can be afforded to the RPD on specific issues when it enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, such an advantage does not arise in the present case.
ANALYSIS

[19] After considering the Appellants' arguments and conducting an independent assessment of the entire record, which includes the transcript of the proceeding before the RPD, I agree with the RPD's determination that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Mumbai.

[20] Refugee claimants are expected to seek protection in another part of their own country, if it is available, before they seek refuge in Canada.8 The notion of an IFA is inherent in the definition of a Convention refugee because refugee protection is a form of surrogate protection.9 Accordingly, the Appellants bear the onus of demonstrating that there is a serious possibility of persecution throughout the country, including the area identified as an IFA.10

Secondly, I must also be satisfied, after considering the Appellants' individual circumstances and the conditions in the proposed IFAs, that it would not be unreasonable to seek refuge in these locations. An IFA will only be viable if both criteria are met.12

The Appellants' state the following in the BOC about the incident on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018: "unknown people attacked in search of by brother-in-law." They similarly state in the BOC that the incidents on XXXX XXXX, & XXXX, 2019, occurred "because of my brother-in-law's [...] (presently in Canada) issues with Dera Sacha Sauda."

[24] I agree with the RPD that the principal Appellant is not credible in his testimony that he was followed and received threatening calls after his brother-in-law's business was looted in XXXX 2017. He testified that: "[f]rom XXXX XXXX this continued happening, for about a year and a half, sometimes people would follow me, sometimes somebody would be coming behind me. Couple of times I was threatened over the phone (sic)." The RPD noted that there is no mention of these allegations in the BOC, and it correctly rejected the principal Appellant's attempt at attributing the omission to his previous representative. The Appellants did not file a complaint against their previous representative and did not amend the BOC to include these allegations despite being represented by new counsel at the hearing. Instead, the principal Appellant's confirmed under oath that the BOC "is complete, true and accurate."

[25] The Federal Court has held that it is reasonable to draw an adverse credibility finding based on an omission from the BOC of important aspects of a claim.13 The omission of incidents which display the agent of harms' direct interest in the Appellants after the looting of the XXXX XXXX is an important allegation to their claims, particularly since these alleged incidents bridge the large gap between the incident at the XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2017, and the incidents at the mother-in-law's home in XXXX 2019. The RPD therefore correctly rejected the principal Appellant's testimony that he was being followed and was receiving threatening telephone calls beginning in XXXX 2017.

[26] The RPD also correctly drew an adverse credibility finding from the contradictory evidence on whether the agents of harm threatened the principal Appellant after XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. The principal Appellant states the following in the BOC: "[a]fter the incident of XXXX XXXX & XXXX, 2019, I was threatened on the phone (sic) that the same will be repeated which they did with [my brother-in-law] and his family." Contrary to this statement in the BOC, when the principal Appellant was asked by the RPD member whether he received "any threats after the visit on the XXXX and XXXX?" he testified that "[n]o, I did not get a threat, but my parents got information that some people are - keep coming around the house. They keep going around, but nobody has said anything." The Appellant provided a third account as an explanation for the inconsistency that involved him receiving threats indirectly through his brother-in-law's social media accounts: "[n]o, these threats were not given on the phone. I did not get those threats directly, but through social media, [my brother-in-law] got that messages (sic)." When the RPD member pointed out that the statement in the BOC refers to the threats by telephone and not through social media, principal Appellant then insisted that "I got the threats only on XXXX and XXXX, but after XXXX I never got any threats," and attributed the inconsistency to his previous counsel.

[27] The Appellants' reliance on the Federal Court decision in Alekozai does not help resolve the inconsistencies between the principal Appellant's testimony and the BOC. The Appellants cite Alekozai for the principle that "discrepancies in testimony relied on to support a finding that the applicant lacked credibility were trivial and did not form a sufficient foundation upon which the applicant's overall credibility could be impugned."14 The discrepancy in Alekozai, however, involved a difference of one day when an event occurred between the claimant's testimony and the notes taken at the port of entry, which the Federal Court classified as trivial.15 In the present case, the principal Appellant provided contradictory evidence on the question of whether he ever followed or received threatening telephone calls, which is not a trivial discrepancy but rather a material contradiction which is central to the question of whether he was ever directly targeted by the agents of harm. Notably, he provided three various and mutually exclusive accounts in his oral testimony which are contrary to the narrative contained in the BOC. In the circumstances, given the extent of the contradictions in the four accounts presented by the principal Appellant, I am not satisfied that he was ever followed or received threatening calls after his brother-in-law's business was looted in XXXX 2017.16

[28] The objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP), notes that the headquarters of the DSS is in Sirsa, Haryana, and its followers are predominantly "lower caste Muslims and Sikhs in the states of Punja, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan."17 The most "significant support" for the DSS is in several districts of the Malwa region of Rajasthan state, where 70 percent of its adherents are found, and its strongest political support appears to be in Punjab state.18

[29] When considering the fact that the agents of harm never directly targeted the Appellants or displayed an interest in them alongside the information in the NDP that displays that the vast majority of DSS adherents are found in Punja, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan states, the evidence does not establish that the agents of harm are motivated to search for the Appellants and pursue them in Mumbai.

[30] For all of the reasons outlined above, based upon my own independent review of the evidence, I am satisfied that the first part of the Rasaratnam test has been met. The Appellants have not shown that they face either a serious possibility of persecution in Mumbai from the DSS, or, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture, a risk to their lives, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
It is reasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Mumbai

[31] I am satisfied that it is reasonable for the Appellants to seek refuge in Mumbai based on their specific circumstances and the objective evidence in the NDP. The Federal Court of Appeal has established, "a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area."19

[32] The RPD considered relevant factors which inform the analysis of whether Mumbai is a reasonable IFA in the Appellants' specific circumstances, including their ability to travel to Mumbai, their language skills, their education and work experience, and the existence of a Sikh community with places of worship. I have not identified any errors in the RPD's analysis based on my independent assessment, and find that its determination is correct. Beyond the foregoing, the objective evidence in the NDP establishes that Sikhs in India are economically and socially integrated, have the freedom to practice their religion, and can rely on local gurdwaras to access housing and other services.20

[33] Both adult Appellants are highly educated and have considerable work experience. The principal Appellant indicates in his sworn schedule A "Background / Declaration" form that he has XXXX years of post-secondary education, with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX, and worked as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX from 2009 to 2016. The adult female associate Appellant similarly has XXXX years of post-secondary education according to her sworn schedule A form, with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX, and worked as a XXXX at tXXXX XXXX XXXX from 2006 to 2010, and from 2011 to 2019. Given the Appellants' education and work history, I do not accept the submission that "there is little support in the record indicating that the claimants would be able to find jobs in the cities identified for the IFAs (sic)."

[34] The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to assess the evidence in a manner that is consistent with the Chairperson Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution, although they have not pointed to evidence that would make Mumbai an unreasonable IFA based on the gender of the two female Appellants. Instead, the Appellants miscategorized the education and work experience of the adult female associate Appellant by submitting that "the female Appellant [...] has only a high school education and no work experience to speak of." This submission is contrary to the evidence in the sworn schedule A as cited above, since the adult female associate Appellant outlines her extensive post-secondary education and work experience as a XXXX. The Okoloise decision which the Appellants cite in support of this argument therefore has no relevance in circumstances of their case, since the Federal Court noted that the female claimant in that case did not have "any previous work experience."21 I have not identified anything in my independent assessment of the record that would make Mumbai an unreasonable IFA for the two female Appellants based on their gender.

[35] Nor is there a basis to determine the minor Appellants' likelihood of persecution or risk of harm in the IFA is different than that of the adult Appellants. There are also no circumstances particular to the minor Appellants, including their ages, that would make Mumbai unreasonable as an IFA, as they will also be under the care and protection of their parents.

[36] For all of the reasons outlined above, after considering all of the Appellants' personal circumstances and Guideline 4, I am satisfied that the second part of the Rasaratnam test has been met and that it would not be objectively unreasonable in the circumstances for the Appellants to relocate to Mumbai.
CONCLUSION

[37] The RPD was correct in its determination that the Appellants have a viable IFA Mumbai. I therefore dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.22
